unit.title: Use and maintain graduated measuring devices

summary: This unit teaches you to choose, use, check and look after the graduated measuring devices used in welding and fabrication: rules and tapes, squares and feeler gauges, protractors, vernier, dial and digital calipers, micrometers, dial indicators, height gauges, gauge blocks, weld gauges and thermometers. You will learn to read each one accurately, avoid the common errors, judge parts against their limits, record and report the results, and run a calibration and care system for your team's devices.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). A **graduated measuring device** is one with a scale (or a digital display) that you read: a steel rule, a tape, a caliper, a micrometer, a dial indicator, a protractor, a weld gauge. At Level 3 you choose the right device for each feature, measure accurately, decide whether work passes, keep the devices in calibration and good condition, and teach others to use them.

A fabrication is only as good as its measurements. A frame cut 3 mm long, a bevel at the wrong angle, an undersize fillet weld or a bore 0.05 mm too small can each mean rework, a failed inspection or a part that will not fit. A device that reads wrong is worse than none, because people trust it.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders, fitters and inspectors who check work and look after the shop's measuring equipment.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Choose the right device
Read the drawing's sizes and tolerances, and pick a device with the range and resolution the job needs.
Check a device before use
Clean it, look for damage, check its zero and its calibration label.
Measure correctly
Use the right pressure, hold it square to the work, read without parallax, measure at the right temperature and from the right datum.
Read every kind of scale
Rules, tapes, verniers, dials, micrometer sleeves and thimbles, protractors and digital displays.
Inspect welds and fit-ups
Use fillet, bridge cam and hi-lo gauges, feeler gauges and squares against the acceptance limits.
Judge, record and report
Compare each reading with its limits, record it with its unit and the device number, and raise a non-conformance report for anything out of limit.
Calibrate and keep records
Check devices against gauge blocks and standards, keep a calibration register and labels, and act when a device fails.
Care for and store devices
Clean, protect and store devices against dust, damp, salt air, heat and magnetism; take damaged devices out of use; train others.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on choosing devices, reading calipers, micrometers, dial indicators and protractors, weld gauges, sources of error, limits, calibration, care, storage and recording.

A **written paper** with short answers (readings to work out, and exact terms such as surface plate, TIR, sleeve, traceability and limits) and essays on planning an inspection, calibrating, training and caring for devices.

Two **group practicals**: planning and carrying out a dimensional and weld inspection of a fabricated item and writing the report; and running a calibration check of the team's devices and setting up a calibration register.

blocks.note: Practise reading real devices, not just pictures. Have a partner set a caliper or micrometer, read it, then check your answer together. Reading errors (especially missing the half-millimetre line on a micrometer) are the commonest mistakes in the exam and on the job.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Measurement basics and choosing a device

ul: Workshop sizes are in **millimetres (mm)**. One **micrometre (µm)** is one thousandth of a millimetre (0.001 mm). Do not confuse the unit, the micrometre, with the instrument, the micrometer.
Angles are in **degrees (°)** and **minutes (′)**: 1° = 60′, so 0.5° = 30′ and 0.25° = 15′.
You will meet inch devices and American drawings: 1 inch = 25.4 mm exactly. Do not mix units in one set of readings.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Resolution
The smallest step the device can show
A digital caliper shows 0.01 mm steps; a tape shows 1 mm
Accuracy
How close a reading is to the true size
A caliper with a stated accuracy of ±0.03 mm may read up to 0.03 mm out, even though it shows 0.01 mm steps
Repeatability (precision)
How closely repeated readings of the same thing agree
Five readings of the same pin: 12.01, 12.02, 12.01, 12.01, 12.02 mm
Range
The sizes the device can measure
A 25–50 mm micrometer measures from 25 mm to 50 mm only

blocks.note: A fine display does not make a device accurate. A digital caliper shows two decimal places, but its accuracy may be only ±0.02 to ±0.03 mm. Always look at the maker's stated accuracy, not just the number of digits.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: The **nominal size** is the size named on the drawing, for example 50 mm.
The **tolerance** is how far the size may vary. It can be equal both ways (50 ± 0.05 mm) or one way (120 +0.0/−0.4 mm).
The **limits** are the largest and smallest sizes allowed. For 50 ± 0.05 mm they are 49.95 mm and 50.05 mm. For 120 +0.0/−0.4 mm they are 120.0 mm and 119.6 mm.
The **tolerance band** is the difference between the limits: 0.10 mm for 50 ± 0.05 mm.

blocks.p: Many workshops choose a device whose **resolution is about one tenth of the tolerance band**. A device much coarser than that cannot tell a good part from a bad one near the limits.

head: Feature on the drawing
Tolerance band
Resolution needed (about band ÷ 10)
Suitable device
rows: Frame length 1,200 ± 5 mm
10 mm
About 1 mm
Steel tape or long steel rule
Plate thickness 10.0 ± 0.5 mm
1.0 mm
About 0.1 mm
Vernier, dial or digital caliper
About 0.01 mm
Inside micrometer or dial bore gauge
About 0.004 mm
Micrometer reading to 0.001 mm
About 0.5°
Bevel protractor

blocks.p: Also choose a device whose **range** fits the size (a 62 mm bar needs a 50–75 mm micrometer), which **reaches** the feature (a bore needs inside jaws, an inside micrometer or a bore gauge), and which suits the conditions (a vernier caliper with no battery for a hot, dusty site).

A **datum** is the edge, face or line that sizes are measured from. If a drawing gives every hole position from edge A, measure every one from edge A. Measuring from a different edge, or from hole to hole, adds the error in each step to the next, so the last hole can be well out even if each step looks close.

Precise sizes, gauge blocks and calibration are all referred to a standard temperature of **20 °C**. Steel grows about **0.012 mm per metre for each 1 °C** rise (stainless steel about 0.017 mm, aluminium about 0.023 mm).

**Worked example:** a 4 m steel beam at 38 °C is 38 − 20 = 18 °C above standard. Growth = 4 × 18 × 0.012 = **0.86 mm**. On a part with a tight tolerance that matters; on a frame with ± 5 mm it does not.

sections.title: Rules, tapes, squares, feeler gauges and protractors

ul: Steel rules are graduated in 1 mm and 0.5 mm. By eye you can read to about 0.5 mm at best.
The end of a rule wears and gets damaged. For accurate work, measure from a clear graduation such as the 10 mm mark and subtract it: a part from 10 mm to 157 mm on the rule is 147 mm long.
Stand the rule on its edge so the graduations touch the work, and look straight down at the mark to avoid **parallax** (reading error from looking at an angle).

The hook on the end slides by its own thickness, so the reading is right both when hooking over an edge (outside) and when pushing against a face (inside). A bent hook or loose rivets give a wrong reading.
For the most accurate long measurements, avoid the hook altogether: hold the 100 mm mark on the datum and subtract 100 mm.
Lay the tape flat along the work and pull it straight with a steady, firm tension. A tape that sags or twists between supports reads long.

Tapes are made to accuracy classes. A guide for steel tapes is: **Class I** about ±(0.1 + 0.1 L) mm and **Class II** about ±(0.3 + 0.2 L) mm, where L is the length in whole metres. Over 12 m that is about ±1.3 mm for Class I and ±2.7 mm for Class II, so check the class against the tolerance before you rely on a tape.

A steel tape and steel work at the **same** temperature grow by about the same amount, so the reading is close to the 20 °C length. Errors come when they are at **different** temperatures (a tape from an air-conditioned office on a beam in the sun), or of different materials.
An **engineer's square** checks that a corner is at 90°. Hold the stock firmly against one face and look for light under the blade against a bright background.
A **feeler gauge** set has thin steel blades of marked thickness (often from about 0.03 mm to 1 mm). Slide blades into a gap until one goes in with a light drag. That blade's thickness is the gap.
To check a set gap, such as a 2.5 mm root gap, stack blades that add up to the size and slide them in; use the fewest blades you can, because each one adds a small error.
Never force a blade, and wipe and lightly oil the set after use; thin blades kink and rust easily.

blocks.p: A **universal bevel protractor** measures angles such as bevel preparations. The main scale is in degrees. A vernier on each side of zero has 12 divisions, each worth **5 minutes (5′)**, because 60′ ÷ 12 = 5′.

flow: Read the whole degrees on the main scale up to the vernier zero
Find the vernier line, on the same side as the main scale is counting, that lines up exactly with a main-scale line
Multiply that line's number by 5′
Add: for example 41° on the main scale and the 7th line (35′) gives 41° 35′

blocks.p: Simple protractors and the angle scale on a weld gauge read in whole degrees or 5° steps: good enough for a bevel of 30° ± 2.5°, not for finer work.

A caliper has a **beam** with a main scale, a **fixed jaw**, and a **sliding jaw**. Most have outside jaws (for thicknesses and diameters), inside jaws (for bores and slots) and a depth rod (for depths of holes and steps). A common size measures 0 to 150 mm.

flow: Read the main scale: the whole millimetres up to the vernier's zero line
Find the one vernier line that lines up exactly with a line on the main scale
Multiply that line's number by the vernier's step (0.05 mm or 0.02 mm, marked on the scale)
Add the two parts together

head: Vernier step
Main scale
Vernier line that lines up
Reading
rows: 24 mm
52 mm

blocks.p: Many verniers are numbered 0 to 10 along their length, each number standing for 0.1 mm, with the 0.05 mm or 0.02 mm lines in between. Read the number before the matching line, then add the lines past it.

A dial caliper shows the whole millimetres on the beam and the fraction on a dial. On the common type, one full turn of the needle is 1 mm and the dial has 100 divisions of 0.01 mm. **Example:** the beam shows 31 mm and the needle points to 27: the reading is 31.27 mm. Some dials are 2 mm per turn: read the marking on the dial face.

ul: They show the reading directly, often to 0.01 mm, and can switch between mm and inches.

They can be **zeroed at any position**. Zero the caliper on a setting piece of known size, then the display shows how much each part differs from it: zeroed on a 25.00 mm setting piece, a display of +0.06 means the part is 25.06 mm. This makes checking a batch quick.

They need a working battery, and they are damaged by water, strong magnetism, and electric current. **Never** let a digital caliper touch work that is being welded or is still connected to the welding return lead: welding current through it can ruin the electronics.

head: Type
Advantages
Drawbacks
rows: Vernier
No battery or gears; tough; keeps its accuracy; works in heat, dust and damp
Slow to read; easy to misread in poor light or with weak eyesight
Dial
Quick to read; no battery
The rack and gears can be damaged by grit or a knock; the needle can jump a tooth, giving a false zero
Digital
Quickest and easiest to read; zero anywhere; mm or inches; fewer reading mistakes in batch work
Needs a battery; can be damaged by water, magnetism and welding current; the display can mislead if the zero is not checked

ul: Clean the jaws and the work; remove burrs and spatter at the measuring point.
Close the jaws and check the zero before you start (0.00 on a digital, the zeros lined up on a vernier, the needle on 0 on a dial), with no light between the jaws.
Put the work **as deep in the jaws, as close to the beam, as they allow**. Any play in the sliding jaw tilts it slightly, and the further from the beam you measure, the bigger the error.
Hold the caliper square to the work, not tilted, and close it with light, even pressure. Do not force it.

For an outside diameter, keep the jaws square to the part's axis: tilted along the axis, the caliper reads large, so the smallest reading as you rock it is the true one. For a bore, the inside jaws must cross the centre: rock them across the bore and take the largest reading.
Read straight on, or lock the jaw and take the caliper away to read it in good light.

blocks.p: A **micrometer** measures more finely than a caliper, usually to 0.01 mm, and some to 0.001 mm. Its parts are the **frame**, the **anvil** (fixed face), the **spindle** (moving face), the **sleeve** (the fixed barrel with the main scale), the **thimble** (which turns), the **ratchet** or friction stop, and the **lock**.

ul: The spindle screw has a pitch of 0.5 mm: one turn of the thimble moves it 0.5 mm.
The sleeve has whole millimetres marked on one side of its line and **half millimetres** on the other.
The thimble has 50 divisions, so each is 0.5 ÷ 50 = **0.01 mm**.

flow: Read the last whole millimetre showing on the sleeve
Add 0.5 mm if a half-millimetre line is showing after it
Add the thimble division that lines up with the sleeve's line, × 0.01 mm
Example: 17 mm + 0.5 mm + 23 × 0.01 mm = 17.73 mm

blocks.note: The commonest micrometer mistake is missing the half-millimetre line: reading 17.23 mm instead of 17.73 mm. Always look for it before you read the thimble.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **vernier micrometer** has a small vernier on the sleeve, usually 10 lines, each worth 0.001 mm. Read the sleeve and thimble as usual, then add the vernier line that lines up with a thimble line, × 0.001 mm. **Example:** 6.5 mm + 31 × 0.01 mm + 7 × 0.001 mm = **6.817 mm**.

ul: Each outside micrometer covers 25 mm: 0–25, 25–50, 50–75, 75–100 mm and so on. Choose the one whose range holds the size.
A 0–25 mm micrometer's zero is checked by closing the clean faces gently with the ratchet: it should read 0.00.
Larger micrometers are checked on the **setting standard** made for them (for example a 25.000 mm rod for a 25–50 mm micrometer).

If it does not read correctly, adjust it as the maker shows, or apply a correction: a micrometer that reads 50.02 mm on its 50.000 mm standard reads 0.02 mm high, so subtract 0.02 mm from readings near that size until it is adjusted. Note any correction on the record.

flow: Clean the faces with a clean, lint-free cloth, and clean the work
Check the zero or the setting standard
Hold the frame by its insulated pad, so hand heat does not make it grow
Open it a little more than the size; place the work square between anvil and spindle
Close it with the **ratchet** until it clicks two or three times, so the pressure is the same every time
Lock it if you need to take it off the work; read the sleeve, then the thimble

ul: Never use the thimble to force the faces onto the work, and never spin the micrometer by its frame to open or close it quickly.

To find taper or out-of-round on a round part, measure at both ends and in two directions at right angles at each end. Different readings at the ends show **taper**; different readings across one end show **out-of-round**.

A **depth micrometer** measures the depth of holes, slots and steps, with interchangeable rods. Its sleeve scale is numbered the opposite way to an outside micrometer, so the reading grows as the thimble is screwed in. Read it carefully, and check it on a known depth before use.
An **inside micrometer**, with extension rods, measures larger bores. Rock it across the bore to find the largest reading, and along the bore to find the smallest; that point is the true diameter.

A **dial bore gauge** is set to size with a ring gauge or a micrometer, then rocked in the bore: the needle turns back at the true diameter, and the dial shows how much the bore differs from the setting.
**Telescopic gauges** are set in the bore, locked, removed and measured with an outside micrometer. Good for odd sizes, but each transfer adds a little error.

sections.title: Dial indicators, height gauges, surface plates and gauge blocks

blocks.p: A **dial indicator** shows small movements of its plunger. On the common metric type, the dial has **100 divisions of 0.01 mm**, one full turn of the needle is **1 mm**, and a small counter dial counts the whole turns.

ul: **Example:** the needle moves 2 full turns and then 35 more divisions: the plunger has moved 2 + 0.35 = 2.35 mm.
Mount the indicator on a rigid stand or magnetic base, never on something that can flex.
Set the plunger **square to the surface**, with a little **pre-load** (pressed in about a quarter of a turn or more) so it can read both up and down. Then turn the bezel to set zero.
A **lever-type indicator** (dial test indicator) has a small swinging stylus. Keep the stylus close to parallel to the surface; at an angle it reads more than the true movement (**cosine error**).

blocks.p: **Run-out** is the wobble of a turning part: a shaft that is bent or off-centre, or a flange face that is not square to its axis. Turn the part slowly through one full turn with the indicator on it and note the highest and lowest readings. The **total indicator reading (TIR)** is the difference between them.

**Example:** the needle swings between −0.02 mm and +0.05 mm. TIR = 0.05 − (−0.02) = **0.07 mm**. Repeat the check, then compare the TIR with the drawing's limit and record it with the position checked.

ul: A **surface plate** is a very flat, heavy plate of granite or cast iron used as the datum (reference surface) for marking out and measuring heights.
Keep it clean and covered when not in use; never hammer, weld, grind or drop work on it; set work down gently.

A **height gauge** (vernier, dial or digital) stands on the surface plate. Zero it on the plate, then raise the scriber or probe to the feature; the reading is its height above the plate. It is used to check hole heights on a bracket, or to mark out lines at a set height.

blocks.p: **Gauge blocks** (slip gauges) are rectangular blocks of hardened steel or ceramic, each made to an exact size, to within a fraction of a micrometre. They are the shop's reference sizes, used to check and set calipers, micrometers and other devices. Sets come in grades: the most accurate are kept for checking other blocks; workshop grades are used for checking instruments.

ul: **Wringing:** clean blocks are slid together with a little pressure so that they cling as one stack. Build a size from the fewest blocks, starting with the block that gives the last decimal places. For example, 41.37 mm: the 1.37 mm block, then blocks making up 40 mm (a single 40 mm block, or 15 + 25 mm, depending on the set).
Handle blocks as little as possible, by their edges, with a clean cloth or gloves. Hand heat makes them grow, and sweat makes them rust.

Never drop them, slide them across each other's faces when dirty, or leave a stack wrung together for long: separate them, clean them, protect them with a light film of the right oil, and put them back in their case.
Let blocks and the device being checked settle to the same temperature before comparing them.

head: Gauge
What it measures
How it is used
rows: Fillet weld gauge
The **leg length** and the **throat** of a fillet weld; whether the face is too convex or concave
A set of leaves, each for one size, or a single gauge with a sliding pointer, held against the plates and the weld face
Bridge cam (multi-purpose) gauge
The angle of a weld preparation, the **cap height** (excess weld metal) of a butt weld, the **depth of undercut** and pitting, fillet throat and leg, and misalignment between plates
Rest it on the plate and turn the cam until its pointer touches the weld or the bottom of the undercut; read the scale
Hi-lo gauge
How far the **inside surfaces** of two pipe ends are out of line at fit-up (hi-lo); some models also measure the root gap and wall thickness
Hook it inside the pipe at the joint and read the step between the two surfaces
Radius gauges
The radius of a corner, or the shape of a weld toe or root
Try blades until one fits with no light showing
Taper gauge and feeler gauges
Root gaps and other small gaps
Slide in until it fits with a light drag; read the size

ul: Check whether the drawing gives the fillet's **leg length** or its **throat thickness**. American (AWS) drawings give the leg; ISO drawings mark the throat with 'a' and the leg with 'z'.
On an equal-leg fillet with a flat face, the throat is about **0.7 × the leg**: a 5 mm leg gives about a 3.5 mm throat.
**Both legs** must be at least the size on the drawing. A weld with one 5 mm leg and one 3.5 mm leg is undersize, whatever the average.
Measure at several places along each weld, especially at starts and stops, after the slag and spatter are removed and the weld has cooled.

blocks.p: Get the drawing and the WPS or specification before you start, so you know the acceptance limit for each feature, for example 'undercut no deeper than 0.5 mm'. A reading beyond the limit is recorded as **out of limit**, the item is marked and kept apart, and it is reported, usually on a **non-conformance report (NCR)**. Never round a reading to make it pass.
Many welding procedures set a **preheat** or a maximum **interpass** temperature, so temperature is measured too.

head: Device
What it gives
Points to know
rows: Contact (surface) thermometer
An actual reading in degrees from a probe touching the steel
Hold the probe flat on clean steel until the reading settles
Infrared (non-contact) thermometer
An actual reading from a distance
Reads low on bright, shiny steel; most accurate on dull, oxidised or painted surfaces; measures a spot that grows bigger with distance
Temperature-indicating crayon
Only whether the steel has reached the crayon's rated temperature
The mark stays dry and chalky below the rating, and melts to a wet, glossy streak at or above it

blocks.p: Measure where the WPS or procedure says, and on both sides of the joint.

head: Error
What happens
How to avoid it
rows: Parallax
Reading a scale from an angle gives the wrong line
Look straight at the scale; use the lock and read in good light
Zero error
The device does not read zero when closed, or reads wrong on its standard
Check the zero before every use; adjust or apply a correction
Too much or uneven pressure
The jaws or faces spring, or the work is squeezed
Use the ratchet on a micrometer and light, even pressure on a caliper
Not square or not deep in the jaws
Tilted jaws, or measuring at the tips, read wrong
Keep the device square and the work close to the beam
Temperature
Hot work or a warm device has grown
Measure at room temperature; let parts and devices settle together; hold devices by their insulated parts
Dirt, burrs, spatter, paint
Something extra is measured
Clean the device and the measuring points
Wear and damage
Worn jaws, a bent tape hook, a sticking slide
Inspect before use; check against standards; take damaged devices out of use
Wrong datum or chain measuring
Small errors add up along the work
Measure from the datum the drawing uses
Sag and tension
A long tape sags or is pulled too hard or too little
Support the tape and use steady tension
Magnetism
A magnetised device picks up filings, which get between the faces
Keep devices away from magnetic bases, lifting magnets and welding leads; demagnetise as the rules allow
Misreading
Missing the half-millimetre line; counting the wrong vernier line
Read twice; have a second person repeat key readings

flow: Look at the calibration label: is it in date?
Look for damage: bent jaws, burrs, a kinked tape, a cracked dial glass, a loose tape hook
Clean the measuring faces with a clean, lint-free cloth
Check that it moves smoothly, and check the zero (or the setting standard)
If it has been dropped or knocked, have it checked before use, even if the label is in date
If anything is wrong, do not use it: tag it, take it out of use and report it
Read the drawing and list every feature to check, with its size and tolerance
Choose a device for each feature (range, resolution, reach, conditions) and note why
Check that each device is clean, zeroed and in calibration
Make sure the item is cool, clean at the measuring points, and not connected to any welding lead
Measure each feature, from the right datum, more than once where it matters
Record each reading and decide accept or reject
Mark, separate and report anything out of limit

blocks.p: A useful record of a measurement shows **the value with its unit, the device's number, who measured it and when**: '24.36 mm, caliper VC-03, K. Brown, 3 November 2026'. A dimensional inspection report also gives:

ul: the job number, the item, the drawing number and its **revision**, and the client;
the devices used, with their numbers and calibration due dates;
a table of each feature, its size and tolerance, the **actual** reading, and accept or reject;
the temperature, where it matters;
the action taken on anything out of limit (an NCR number, a repair);
the inspector's signature and date, and the supervisor's review.

blocks.note: Write the actual size, not just 'OK'. 49.96 mm on a 50 ± 0.05 mm feature passes, but it shows the work is close to its limit, and a run of such readings shows a trend before parts start to fail.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: If an inspection finds parts out of limit (for example 3 of 20 brackets too long), label them and set them aside so they cannot be used by mistake, record the readings, and report them through a non-conformance report. Check whether the cause could affect other parts, such as a stop on the saw set wrongly.

**Calibration** is comparing a device with a standard of known, better accuracy, and recording the errors. **Traceability** is the unbroken chain of comparisons that links the shop's device to the national and international measurement standards: the shop's caliper is checked against the shop's gauge blocks, the gauge blocks are calibrated by an accredited laboratory, and that laboratory's standards are traced to the national standards.

ul: Send the shop's reference standards (gauge blocks, setting standards, reference tape) to an **accredited calibration laboratory** at set intervals. In Jamaica, laboratories are accredited by the Jamaica National Agency for Accreditation (JANAAC).

A **calibration certificate** identifies the device (number, serial number), the laboratory, the date, the standards used, the conditions, and the **error found at each test point**, often with the measurement uncertainty.
In-house checks of working devices against those standards can then be done by trained staff, and recorded.

blocks.p: Every graduated device used by the team is listed in a **register** (on paper or a spreadsheet):

head: Column
Example
rows: Device number
MIC-04 (also marked on the device or its case)
Description, range and resolution
Outside micrometer, 25–50 mm, 0.01 mm
Where it is kept
Inspection cabinet, shelf 2
Check interval
6 months
Last check: date, results, pass or fail, by whom
3 November 2026: largest error 0.004 mm, pass, D. Thomas
Next due date

blocks.p: The **interval** depends on how much the device is used, how accurate it must be, and its past results: a busy caliper might be checked every three months, a little-used protractor once a year. Each device carries a **status label** with its number, the date checked, the next due date and who checked it.

blocks.h: An in-house check of a caliper

flow: Work in a clean, cool place; leave the caliper and the gauge blocks together until they are the same temperature
Clean the jaws; look for damage, burrs or a bent jaw; check that the slide moves smoothly
Close the jaws: check the zero, and that no light shows between them
Measure gauge blocks with the outside jaws at several points across the range (for example about 10, 50, 100 and 150 mm), held deep in the jaws
Check the inside jaws on a ring gauge or a set size, and the depth rod on a block on the surface plate
For each point record the true size, the reading and the error (error = reading − true size)
Compare each error with the limit, then label it, or tag it 'Do not use' and report it

blocks.p: **Example:** on a 50.000 mm block the caliper reads 49.98 mm, an error of −0.02 mm. If the limit is ±0.03 mm, it passes at that point.

Micrometers are checked the same way, at their zero or setting standard and then at several sizes across the range chosen so the thimble sits at different positions (for example 5.1, 10.3, 15.0, 20.2 and 25.0 mm on a 0–25 mm micrometer).

blocks.h: When a device fails or is overdue

ul: Tag it **'Do not use'**, take it out of service, record it in the register, and report it.
Have it adjusted, repaired or replaced by a competent person or the supplier. Trainees never try to repair a measuring device.
**Review the work measured with it** since its last good check: parts accepted with a device that reads wrong may be faulty, and may need re-checking or recalling.
Do not use an overdue device: use another one that is in date, and report the overdue one.

blocks.p: Jamaica's warm, humid and often salty air rusts bare steel fast, and a welding shop adds dust, grinding grit, spatter, heat and magnetism.

head: When
What to do
rows: After each use
Wipe off dust, grit, oil and fingerprints with a clean cloth
Put a very light film of instrument oil on bare steel parts
Return the device to its case: micrometer faces slightly apart, lock released; caliper jaws slightly open, unlocked
Wipe a tape dry before winding it in, and let it wind in slowly so the hook is not damaged
Switch off digital devices
Storage
Cases in a closed cabinet, away from welding bays, grinding and spatter
Drying sachets (silica gel) in the cabinet help keep the air dry
Away from magnetic bases, lifting magnets and welding leads
Remove batteries from digital devices that will not be used for a long time
Each week (team leader)
Check every device: zero, smooth movement, clear scales, tape hooks and blades, batteries, labels
Remove light rust gently and re-oil; demagnetise as the maker and the rules allow
When damaged or out of limit
Tag 'Do not use', record in the register, send for repair or replace

blocks.p: A micrometer is stored with its faces slightly apart so that changes in temperature cannot strain the frame and the faces against each other. Never use a measuring device as a hammer, a clamp, a scriber or a lever, and never measure work that is moving or still hot.

flow: **Explain:** what the device is for, its range and resolution, and its parts
**Demonstrate:** cleaning, the zero check and a measurement, reading the scale out loud
**Practise:** the learner measures while you watch and correct (pressure, squareness, reading)

**Assess:** the learner measures pieces whose sizes you already know, without help; if every reading agrees within one division and the device is cleaned and stored correctly, sign them off on the training record

blocks.p: If a team member uses a device wrongly (for example reading a caliper with the work at the jaw tips and the caliper tilted), stop them, show the right method, and have them measure again.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain resolution, accuracy, repeatability and range, and tell a micrometer from a micrometre.
I can work out limits and tolerance bands, and choose a device using the rule of ten.
I can measure from the datum the drawing uses, and allow for temperature.
I can use and read a steel rule, a tape, a square, feeler gauges and a bevel protractor.
I can read vernier, dial and digital calipers, and use a digital caliper to compare parts with a setting piece.
I can read outside micrometers to 0.01 mm and 0.001 mm, check their zero, and apply a correction.
I can use depth and inside micrometers, bore gauges and telescopic gauges.
I can find taper and out-of-round on a round part.
I can set up a dial indicator and find the TIR of a turning part.
I can use a surface plate and a height gauge, and handle and wring gauge blocks.
I can check fillet and butt welds with fillet, bridge cam and hi-lo gauges against the acceptance limits.
I can measure preheat with a contact thermometer, an infrared thermometer or crayons, and know what each tells me.
I can name the sources of measuring error and avoid them.
I can check a device before use and plan an inspection.
I can record readings properly, judge accept or reject, and report parts that are out of limit.
I can explain calibration and traceability, and read a calibration certificate.
I can run an in-house check of a caliper or micrometer and keep a calibration register.
I can act correctly when a device fails, is damaged or is overdue.
I can clean, protect and store devices in a humid, salty, dusty welding shop.
I can teach a team member to use a device and check that they are competent.

terms: How close a reading is to the true size
Comparing a device with a better standard and recording its errors
A reading error when an indicator's plunger or stylus is at an angle to the surface
The edge, face or line that sizes are measured from
Hardened blocks made to exact sizes, used as reference standards; also called slip gauges
The misalignment between the inside surfaces of two pipe ends at a joint
The largest and smallest sizes a feature may be
A reading error caused by looking at a scale from an angle
The part of a micrometer that slips at a set force, so every reading uses the same pressure
The smallest step a device can show
Choose a device whose resolution is about one tenth of the tolerance band
The wobble of a turning part, measured with a dial indicator
A piece of exact size used to check or set a micrometer's zero
The fixed part of a micrometer, under the thimble, carrying the scale in 0.5 mm steps
A very flat granite or cast iron plate used as a reference surface
The turning part of a micrometer, with 50 divisions of 0.01 mm
Total indicator reading: the difference between the highest and lowest dial readings in one turn
How far a size may vary from its nominal size
The unbroken chain of comparisons linking a device to the national measurement standards
A small sliding scale that lets a main scale be read more finely
Sliding clean gauge blocks together so that they cling as one stack

c1.title: Pump shaft sleeves in Ocho Rios
c1.text: Devon works at an engineering shop in Ocho Rios, St Ann, that repairs hotel water pumps. He must check 10 stainless-steel shaft sleeves that have just come off the lathe, still warm. Each is drawn as 42.00 mm +0.00/−0.04 mm outside diameter. The shop has a 0–150 mm digital caliper (resolution 0.01 mm, stated accuracy ±0.03 mm) and a 25–50 mm outside micrometer reading to 0.01 mm, with its setting standard.

c2.title: Solar-heater frames for hotels in Negril
c2.text: Annmarie is inspecting 25 welded frames that will hold solar water heaters on hotel roofs in Negril, Westmoreland. The drawing calls for 5 mm fillet welds (leg length), and the specification allows undercut no deeper than 0.5 mm. She has a fillet weld gauge, a bridge cam gauge and a digital caliper. The bridge cam gauge's calibration label shows it was due for checking last month; the training centre has a second bridge cam gauge that is in date.

c3.title: Calibration day in St Ann's Bay
c3.text: Chevaughn is checking a training centre's measuring devices in St Ann's Bay before a new intake. The devices have been on a sunny window ledge all morning; the gauge blocks have been in a cool cabinet. A 0–150 mm vernier caliper reading to 0.02 mm reads 0.00 with the jaws closed, and 49.98 mm on a 50.000 mm gauge block. The centre's limit for this caliper is ±0.03 mm. The centre sends its gauge blocks to an accredited laboratory every year.

c4.title: A roof beam in Ewarton
c4.text: Orane must check the length of a steel roof beam for a warehouse being built in Ewarton, St Catherine. The drawing gives 12,000 mm ± 3 mm. At 1 p.m. the beam has been in full sun and is at about 35 °C. He has a 15 m Class I steel tape, calibrated last month, which has been lying on the beam in the sun. Steel grows about 0.012 mm per metre for each 1 °C.

c5.title: A humid shop in Port Antonio
c5.text: At a fabrication shop in Port Antonio, Portland, a few metres from the sea, the measuring devices are kept on an open shelf beside the welding bays. Keisha, the new team leader, finds a vernier caliper with rust spots on its beam, and a dial caliper whose needle no longer comes back to zero when the jaws are closed.

questions.q: Which device should Devon use for the sleeve diameters, and why?
o: The caliper: its 0.01 mm display is fine enough
The micrometer: the caliper's error is most of the band
The caliper: it can be zeroed at any point along its beam
Either one, since both of them read to 0.01 mm
questions.why: The tolerance band is only 0.04 mm. A caliper that may be 0.03 mm out cannot tell a good sleeve from a bad one near the limits, even though it shows 0.01 mm steps. The micrometer is far more accurate for this job.

questions.q: On a cooled sleeve, the micrometer's sleeve scale shows 41.5 mm and the thimble reads 47. What is the size, and is it acceptable?
o: 41.47 mm: rejected
42.47 mm: rejected
41.97 mm: rejected
41.97 mm: accepted
questions.why: 41.5 mm + 47 × 0.01 mm = 41.97 mm. The limits of 42.00 +0.00/−0.04 mm are 41.96 mm and 42.00 mm, so 41.97 mm is inside them. 41.47 mm comes from missing the half-millimetre line.

questions.q: One sleeve measures 41.98 mm at one end and 41.95 mm at the other. What does this show?
o: It is tapered, and the small end is below the lower limit
It is out of round, but both ends are inside the limits
The micrometer has a zero error of 0.03 mm to correct
Both readings are close, so record the average and pass it
questions.why: Different readings at the two ends show taper. The lower limit is 41.96 mm, so the 41.95 mm end is under size and the sleeve is rejected. Averaging hides the fault. Out-of-round shows as different readings across one end.

questions.q: Why should Devon let the sleeves cool before the final measurement?
o: Warm metal has grown, so it would measure over size
Warm metal shrinks, so it would measure under size
The micrometer's ratchet will not click on warm parts
Warm parts make the micrometer's thimble scale fade
questions.why: Metal expands as it warms, and stainless steel grows faster than mild steel. With a band of only 0.04 mm, a few degrees can move a reading noticeably, so final checks are made at room temperature.

questions.q: Which check needs the bridge cam gauge, because the fillet weld gauge cannot make it?
o: The leg length of each fillet weld
Whether each fillet face is convex or concave
The depth of undercut at the weld toe
The throat size of each fillet weld
questions.why: A fillet weld gauge checks leg length, throat and face shape. The bridge cam gauge's cam pointer reaches into the groove to measure undercut depth, which is needed here against the 0.5 mm limit.

questions.q: On one weld the fillet gauge shows one leg of 5 mm and the other of 3.5 mm. What should Annmarie record?
o: 5 mm, since one leg reaches the size on the drawing
Both legs, with the weld marked as undersize
4.25 mm, the average of the two leg lengths
Accepted, since the throat looks about right
questions.why: Both legs of a fillet weld must be at least the size on the drawing. Recording both readings shows exactly what is wrong; averaging or recording only the good leg would pass a weld that does not meet the drawing.

questions.q: The bridge cam gauge she picked up is past its calibration due date. What should she do?
o: Use it anyway, since weld gauges have no moving parts to wear
Use it, but write 'approx.' beside each undercut reading
Use the in-date gauge, and report the overdue one
Check the due date again next month, then decide what to do
questions.why: Results taken with an overdue device cannot be trusted or defended. Use a device that is in date, and report the overdue one so it is checked and its register entry updated.

questions.q: On an equal-leg, flat-faced fillet weld with 5 mm legs, about what throat should the gauge show?
o: About 2.5 mm
About 3.5 mm
About 5.0 mm
About 7.1 mm
questions.why: On an equal-leg fillet with a flat face, the throat is about 0.7 × the leg: 0.7 × 5 = 3.5 mm. 7.1 mm would come from multiplying by 1.41 instead of dividing.

questions.q: Before comparing the devices with the gauge blocks, what should Chevaughn do?
o: Warm the gauge blocks in his hands until they match the devices
Start at once, since temperature matters only for long parts
Oil the gauge blocks heavily so that they slide more easily
Let devices and blocks settle to the same temperature
questions.why: Devices from a sunny ledge are warmer, and have grown, compared with blocks from a cool cabinet. Letting them settle together removes that error. Warming blocks in the hand adds error and leaves sweat that causes rust.

questions.q: Does the vernier caliper pass at 50 mm?
o: Yes: it reads 0.02 mm low, inside the ±0.03 mm limit
No: any error at all means a caliper fails its check
No: it reads 0.02 mm low, so it must be adjusted first
Yes: an error of 0.20 mm is small on a 150 mm caliper
questions.why: Error = reading − true size = 49.98 − 50.000 = −0.02 mm: it reads 0.02 mm low. That is within the ±0.03 mm limit, so it passes at that point, and the error is recorded on the check sheet.

questions.q: Why does the centre send its gauge blocks to an accredited laboratory each year?
o: Because gauge blocks wear out completely after a single year of use
So that the laboratory can grind each block back to its true size
Because gauge blocks gradually lose their magnetism
So that the blocks, and devices checked with them, are traceable
questions.why: The blocks are the centre's reference. Calibrating them at an accredited laboratory links them, and every caliper and micrometer checked against them, to the national measurement standards: that is traceability.

questions.q: The caliper passes. What should its status label show?
o: Its number, the date checked, the next due date and who checked it
Only the word 'OK', so that users can see at a glance that it is fine
The price and the supplier, for when it needs to be replaced
The name of the last trainee who used it before the check
questions.why: The label lets every user see at once whether the device is in date and who is responsible, and it matches the device to its entry in the calibration register.

questions.q: How much longer is the beam at 35 °C than it would be at 20 °C?
o: About 0.2 mm
About 2.2 mm
About 5.0 mm
About 22 mm
questions.why: The beam is 35 − 20 = 15 °C above standard: 12 m × 15 × 0.012 mm = 2.16 mm, about 2.2 mm. Using 35 °C instead of the 15 °C difference gives the wrong figure of about 5.0 mm.

questions.q: The tape has been lying on the beam and is at the same temperature. What does this mean for Orane's reading?
o: The reading is 2.2 mm too long, so he must subtract it
The reading is 2.2 mm too short, so he must add it
Both grew about equally, so the error largely cancels
A warm tape cannot be used, so he must measure at night
questions.why: A steel tape and a steel beam at the same temperature grow by about the same proportion, so the tape reads close to the beam's 20 °C length. The error comes when tape and work are at different temperatures.

questions.q: Orane's reading, with tape and beam at the same temperature, is 12,001 mm. Is the beam's length acceptable?
o: No: it must be exactly 12,000 mm to pass
Yes: it lies between 11,997 mm and 12,003 mm
No: it is longer than the length on the drawing
Only after he subtracts 2.2 mm for the heat
questions.why: 12,000 mm ± 3 mm gives limits of 11,997 mm and 12,003 mm, and 12,001 mm is inside them. No heat correction is needed, because the tape and the beam grew together.

questions.q: Why is a Class I tape a better choice than a Class II tape for this check?
o: Class I tapes do not grow at all when they are in the sun
Class II tapes may not be used on any structural steelwork
A Class I tape can be read accurately without its end hook
A Class II tape could be out by about ±2.7 mm over 12 m
questions.why: By the class guide, a Class II tape may be out by about ±(0.3 + 0.2 × 12) = ±2.7 mm over 12 m, nearly the whole ±3 mm tolerance. A Class I tape, about ±1.3 mm, leaves room to judge the beam.

questions.q: What should Keisha do about the dial caliper whose needle no longer returns to zero?
o: Reset the bezel to zero before each reading and keep using it
Oil the rack heavily so that the gears run freely again
Tag it 'Do not use' and send it to be checked and repaired
Tap it on the bench until the needle settles back on zero
questions.why: A needle that will not return to zero suggests grit in the rack, a damaged gear or a jumped tooth, so its readings cannot be trusted. It is taken out of use, recorded in the register and repaired by a competent person.

questions.q: Which daily routine best protects the steel devices in this salty, humid shop?
o: Wipe them clean, oil bare steel lightly and put them in their cases
Wash them in fresh water at the end of each day to remove salt
Leave them out in the sun each afternoon so that they dry out
Coat them thickly in grease once a week and leave them on the shelf
questions.why: Cleaning off dust and fingerprints, a very light film of instrument oil, and closed cases in a cabinet away from the welding bays keep rust off. Water and heat cause rust and errors, and thick grease traps grit.

questions.q: On a caliper whose vernier is divided into 0.02 mm steps, the vernier's zero sits just past 36 on the beam, and line 17 of the vernier matches a beam line. What size does it show?
questions.why: 36 mm + 17 × 0.02 mm = 36 + 0.34 = 36.34 mm. 36.85 mm would come from a 0.05 mm vernier, and 36.17 mm from reading the line number as hundredths.

questions.q: A temperature-indicating crayon rated at 150 °C leaves a dry, chalky mark on the plate. What does this tell you?
o: The plate is below 150 °C
The plate is above 150 °C
The plate is exactly 150 °C
The crayon is past its use-by date
questions.why: The crayon's mark melts to a wet, glossy streak when the steel is at or above its rated temperature. A dry mark means the plate has not yet reached 150 °C; a crayon cannot give an actual reading, as a thermometer does.
